## S4 · Q18 — Flaw

**Correct answer:** B

### Stimulus
Lindsey: Several people claim that our company was unfair when it failed to give bonuses to the staff. Perhaps they recalled that the company had promised that if it increased its profits over last year's, the staff would all get bonuses. However, the company's profit was much smaller this year than it was last year. Clearly, then, the company acted fairly.

### Prompt
The argument is flawed in that it

### Standard
**Conclusion (clearly, then)**
The company acted fairly in failing to give bonuses to the staff.

**Evidence**
Some people claim the company was unfair, perhaps because they recall that the company promised that if profits were higher than last year's, the staff would get bonuses.

But profits were much smaller than last year's.

**Evaluate**
Whenever we're doing Flaw and the author is rebutting some other position and concluding the polar opposite position, we want to be thinking about the famous Unproven vs. Proven False flaw.

EXAMPLE - Some people claim that cell phones cause cancer. But no scientific study has ever determined this. Thus, cell phones do not cause cancer.

The flaw here is that even though someone else failed to prove that cell phones DO cause cancer, that doesn't mean the author has presented any evidence that proves cell phones DON'T cause cancer.

In this argument, some people claim "the company acted unfairly" in failing to give the staff bonuses. Our author ends up concluding "the company acted fairly", and this is not by presenting positive evidence of her own in favor of this conclusion.

Instead, she's just taking down the argument that (she thinks) was being made in favor of the opposite conclusion.

**Goal**
The author should be responding to the actual reasons these several people offered in defense of their claim that the company was unfair, not speculating that "Perhaps they were basing their claim on X". So an answer might complain about that.

Even if the author is correct, and the people were basing their argument on X, the fact that the author has shown that X is not a valid way to prove "Unfair" doesn't suddenly mean that the author has proven "Fair". This is more in the Unproven vs. Proven False vein.

**Answer choices**
**A. relies on the opinions of certain unnamed people without establishing that those people were well informed on the matter** — Bad Evidence Match (14% of students)
This answer describes a flaw involving reliance on unnamed or poorly informed authorities. But Lindsey does not rely on unnamed sources to build her OWN case — she responds to other people's complaint by challenging their reasoning. The issue is not WHO is making the complaint or whether they are well-informed. The issue is HOW Lindsey responds to the complaint. She defeats one reason for the opinion and concludes the opinion is false. The flaw is structural (incomplete refutation), not epistemic (unreliable sources). Even if the complainers were perfectly informed experts, Lindsey's logical error would be identical.

**B. infers that an opinion is false merely because one potential reason for that opinion has been undermined** — Correct (57% of students)
This answer precisely identifies Lindsey's logical error. People claimed the company's decision was unfair, and one supporting reason was that the company had large profits (or profits had increased). Lindsey showed that this particular reason is factually weak — profits were actually smaller. So far, so good. But then she makes the leap: since this one reason is undermined, the entire opinion must be wrong, and the company acted fairly.

This is a textbook incomplete refutation. An opinion can rest on multiple independent reasons. The employees might believe the decision was unfair because of contractual promises, precedent, management compensation, industry norms, or other factors Lindsey never addresses. By treating one challenged reason as the entire foundation for the opinion, Lindsey dramatically overstates what her evidence accomplishes. She refuted one premise and concluded she had refuted the conclusion — but conclusions can survive the loss of a single supporting reason if other reasons remain intact.

**C. dismisses a claim on the basis of certain irrelevant attributes of the people who made the claim** — Wrong Flaw (2% of students)
This answer describes an ad hominem fallacy — dismissing a claim by attacking the character or attributes of the people making it rather than addressing the substance. But Lindsey does not attack the complainers personally. She does not question their intelligence, motives, credibility, or character. Instead, she directly engages with one factual claim they rely on (the profit level) and attempts to refute it. Lindsey's flaw is different: she engages with the substance but treats her rebuttal of one supporting reason as a complete refutation of the opinion. She deserves credit for engaging with the argument — she just does so in a logically incomplete way.

**D. confuses the size of a quantity with the amount by which that quantity has increased** — Bad Evidence Match (22% of students)
This answer accuses Lindsey of confusing the size of profits with the amount by which profits increased — conflating absolute levels with rates of change. But Lindsey does not make this mathematical error. Her argument about profits is straightforward: people thought profits were large (or had increased), and Lindsey points out that profits were actually much smaller. She does not mix up "total profits" with "profit growth." Her error lies elsewhere — in the logical leap from "one reason for the opinion is wrong" to "the opinion itself is wrong." This answer identifies a mathematical confusion that is not present in the argument.

**E. overlooks the possibility that a policy can be fair even when it is not generous** — Not Present (5% of students)
This answer suggests Lindsey conflates fairness with generosity — perhaps arguing the company was fair when the real issue is that it was not generous. But Lindsey does not slide between these concepts. She directly argues the company's decision was fair, and the complainers directly argue it was unfair. Neither side introduces or confuses the concept of generosity. Lindsey's actual flaw is structural: she shows one reason for the unfairness claim is wrong and leaps to the conclusion that the company acted fairly. This is an incomplete refutation error, not a semantic confusion between "fair" and "generous." The flaw described in this answer simply is not present in Lindsey's reasoning.

### Brief
**Conclusion**
Lindsey concludes the company acted fairly in not paying bonuses.

**Evidence**
People claimed unfairness, perhaps recalling a promise of bonuses if profits increased. But profits were actually much smaller this year.

**Evaluate**
Lindsey disproves one potential reason for the unfairness opinion (large profits) and concludes the opinion itself is wrong. But other valid reasons for unfairness could exist that she never addresses.

**Goal**
Find the answer that identifies the flaw of treating one defeated reason as a refutation of the entire opinion.

**Answer choices**
**A. relies on the opinions of certain unnamed people without establishing that those people were well informed on the matter** — Bad Evidence Match (14% of students)
Lindsey's flaw is not about relying on unnamed people. She engages with the substance of the complaint — her error is in treating one defeated reason as a complete refutation. The identity of the complainers is irrelevant.

**B. infers that an opinion is false merely because one potential reason for that opinion has been undermined** — Correct (57% of students)
Lindsey undermines one reason for the "unfair" opinion (profits were large) and concludes the opinion is wrong. But other valid reasons for unfairness could exist that she never addresses. Defeating one reason does not defeat the opinion.

**C. dismisses a claim on the basis of certain irrelevant attributes of the people who made the claim** — Wrong Flaw (2% of students)
Lindsey does not attack the people making the complaint. She engages with their reasoning about profits. Her error is incomplete refutation, not ad hominem.

**D. confuses the size of a quantity with the amount by which that quantity has increased** — Bad Evidence Match (22% of students)
Lindsey does not confuse profit size with profit growth. Her point about profits is straightforward. Her actual error is treating one refuted reason as a complete refutation of the opinion.

**E. overlooks the possibility that a policy can be fair even when it is not generous** — Not Present (5% of students)
Lindsey does not equivocate between "fair" and "generous." She directly argues fairness. Her flaw is treating one refuted reason as a complete refutation, not confusing related concepts.

### Another Way
**Conclusion**
Lindsey declares the company acted fairly. Case closed, gavel banged.

**Evidence**
People complained about no bonuses. Lindsey says they probably think profits were big — but actually, profits were smaller this year. Therefore: fair!

**Evaluate**
Lindsey knocked down ONE reason for the complaint and declared total victory. That's like a restaurant getting one bad review dismissed and claiming all criticism is invalid. Maybe the employees have a dozen reasons to call the decision unfair — contractual promises, tradition, the CEO's new yacht — and Lindsey addressed exactly one. Winning a single battle is not winning the war.

**Goal**
Find the answer that nails this specific flaw: treating one undermined reason as a complete refutation of the opinion it supported.

**Answer choices**
**A. relies on the opinions of certain unnamed people without establishing that those people were well informed on the matter** — Bad Evidence Match (14% of students)
This answer is worried about WHO is complaining — are they named? Credible? Do they have insider knowledge? None of that matters. Lindsey's error isn't about the complainers' credentials. It's about her reasoning strategy: knock down one reason, declare total victory. She could be debating Nobel laureates or random strangers — the logical mistake would be exactly the same. Focus on HOW she argues, not WHO she's arguing with.

**B. infers that an opinion is false merely because one potential reason for that opinion has been undermined** — Correct (57% of students)
Imagine a restaurant gets a review saying: "Terrible — cold food, rude waiters, cockroaches, two-hour wait." Lindsey proves the food was actually warm. "See?" she announces. "The restaurant is GREAT!" But the rude waiters? The cockroaches? The endless wait? Lindsey kicked out one leg and declared the chair couldn't stand. People might have a dozen reasons to call the bonus decision unfair, and Lindsey addressed exactly one. That's not winning an argument — that's winning a skirmish and declaring world peace.

**C. dismisses a claim on the basis of certain irrelevant attributes of the people who made the claim** — Wrong Flaw (2% of students)
An ad hominem would be Lindsey saying "those complainers are just lazy whiners who don't understand business." But she doesn't go there — she actually tries to engage with their factual claims. She talks about profits, not personalities. Her problem is that she thinks dismantling one piece of evidence destroys the whole case. Not mean-spirited, just logically overconfident. The wrong flaw label for the right kind of mistake.

**D. confuses the size of a quantity with the amount by which that quantity has increased** — Bad Evidence Match (22% of students)
This answer accuses Lindsey of mixing up "how big profits are" with "how much they grew." But that's not her mistake — she handles the profit numbers just fine. Her error is more fundamental: she thinks correcting one data point invalidates an entire opinion. It's like accusing someone of confusing miles with kilometers when their actual mistake was driving to the wrong city. Close in subject matter, but identifying the wrong specific error.

**E. overlooks the possibility that a policy can be fair even when it is not generous** — Not Present (5% of students)
Fair versus generous — is Lindsey really playing word games between these two concepts? Nope. She says "the company acted fairly" and means it at face value. No semantic trickery, no concept-switching. Her actual mistake is much more straightforward: she knocked down one reason for the complaint and declared the entire debate over. Don't overcomplicate the diagnosis when the disease is simple. The flaw is logical overreach, not vocabulary confusion.

## S4 · Q19 — Paradox

**Correct answer:** E

### Stimulus
It is widely known that the rescue squads serving high mountain areas with treacherous weather save the lives of many mountain climbers every year. However, many experienced climbers believe that the rising annual toll of deaths and injuries among climbers in these regions can be significantly reduced only by completely abolishing the rescue squads.

### Prompt
Which one of the following, if true, would most help to justify the apparently paradoxical belief of the experienced climbers?

### Standard
**Given that ...**
It's widely known that rescue squads save the lives of lots of mountain climbers every year.

**How can it be that ...**
A lot of experienced climbers think that the only way to significantly reduce climbing deaths and injuries among climbers is to abolish the rescue squad.

**Evaluate**
Since we know rescue squads save the lives of climbers, how would getting rid of the rescue squad lead to fewer climbing deaths and injuries?

There must something else different in a world without rescue squads that would lead to fewer climbing deaths and injuries. Maybe having a rescue squad emboldens people to take risks they wouldn't otherwise take. It's like if you take away the safety net from a trapeze, a lot fewer people are going to attempt the trapeze, and so maybe you get a net reduction in trapeze injuries.

**Goal**
Look for something that would be different in a world without rescue squads, that could help explain fewer climbing deaths and injuries.

**Answer choices**
**A. It is difficult to recruit and train members for the rescue squads.** — No Impact (4% of students)
Difficulty recruiting members for rescue squads is an operational staffing challenge that has no bearing on the paradox. The question is not about whether rescue squads are hard to maintain — it is about why their existence correlates with more deaths and injuries. Even if recruitment were effortless, the paradox would remain. This answer addresses the wrong question entirely: it discusses why squads are difficult to run, not why their presence might cause net harm.

**B. The recording of deaths and injuries tends to be more accurate in mountain regions served by rescue squads.** — No Impact (8% of students)
This answer suggests that mountains with rescue squads simply have more thorough record-keeping, making deaths and injuries appear higher when they may not actually be. While this is a reasonable real-world observation, resolve-the-paradox questions require accepting both facts as true and finding a way to reconcile them. If the higher numbers are merely a recording artifact, then the premise is wrong rather than paradoxical. The question asks us to explain why experienced climbers genuinely believe abolishing squads would reduce casualties — not to dispute the data underlying their belief.

**C. People who commonly take risks with their lives and health do not expect other people to take those risks to rescue them.** — Opposite (10% of students)
This answer states that people who take the most extreme risks on mountains do so regardless of whether rescue squads are present. If the most reckless climbers' behavior is unchanged by rescue squads, then removing squads would leave the same reckless climbers on the mountain but without anyone to save them. That would increase deaths, not decrease them. This answer actually strengthens the case for keeping rescue squads rather than explaining why they should be abolished. The correct resolution requires rescue squads to change the composition of who climbs, which this answer explicitly denies for the most dangerous subgroup.

**D. Most of the people injured or killed while mountain climbing were not adequately prepared for the dangers they would face.** — No Distinction (13% of students)
This answer tells us that most of the people who get injured on mountains with rescue squads were inadequately prepared. That is a useful description of the casualty profile, but it is incomplete as a resolution. The critical question remains unanswered: why are unprepared people attempting dangerous climbs in the first place? This answer provides the "what" without the "because." It would need one additional logical step — that rescue squads' presence encouraged these unprepared climbers to attempt the climb — to actually resolve the paradox. As stated, it describes a pattern in the casualties without explaining the cause of that pattern.

**E. The lower the risk of climbing a particular mountain is perceived to be, the greater the number of less competent climbers who attempt to climb it.** — Correct (64% of students)
This answer provides the complete causal chain that resolves the paradox. When rescue squads are present, the perceived risk of climbing decreases. Lower perceived risk encourages a much larger number of less competent climbers to attempt the mountain — people who would not have tried it without the safety net. These inexperienced climbers get into dangerous situations at a high rate. Even though rescue squads save some of them, the massive increase in the number of at-risk climbers produces a net increase in total deaths and injuries. This is the moral hazard principle: a safety mechanism that changes behavior in ways that increase overall risk. The squads do not just help existing climbers — they change the composition of who climbs.

### Brief
**Paradox**
Rescue squads save many climbers' lives every year. Yet experienced climbers believe the rising toll of deaths and injuries can be significantly reduced only by completely abolishing rescue squads.

**Evaluate**
If rescue squads save lives, abolishing them should cause more deaths — not fewer. Something about the squads' existence must be increasing the total number of casualties more than their rescues reduce it.

**Goal**
Find the answer that explains how life-saving rescue squads could paradoxically lead to a higher overall death toll.

**Answer choices**
**A. It is difficult to recruit and train members for the rescue squads.** — No Impact (4% of students)
Difficulty recruiting squad members does not explain why rescue squads lead to more deaths. Staffing challenges are irrelevant to the paradox about climber behavior.

**B. The recording of deaths and injuries tends to be more accurate in mountain regions served by rescue squads.** — No Impact (8% of students)
Better record-keeping near squads would explain higher reported numbers but does not resolve the paradox. The question presents the higher death rate as real, not as a data artifact.

**C. People who commonly take risks with their lives and health do not expect other people to take those risks to rescue them.** — Opposite (10% of students)
If extreme risk-takers climb regardless of rescue availability, then removing squads just means fewer rescues for the same reckless behavior. This makes the paradox harder to explain, not easier.

**D. Most of the people injured or killed while mountain climbing were not adequately prepared for the dangers they would face.** — No Distinction (13% of students)
Saying most victims were inadequately prepared describes the problem without explaining why those unprepared people attempted the climb. It identifies the "who" but not the "why."

**E. The lower the risk of climbing a particular mountain is perceived to be, the greater the number of less competent climbers who attempt to climb it.** — Correct (64% of students)
Rescue squads lower perceived risk, attracting incompetent climbers who would not otherwise attempt the climb. The flood of unprepared climbers creates more total casualties than the squads can prevent — classic moral hazard.

### Another Way
**Paradox**
Rescue squads are heroes. They save lives. Nobody disputes that. But the people who actually KNOW mountains — experienced climbers — are saying "get rid of them entirely." That sounds insane, like firefighters petitioning to close fire stations.

**Evaluate**
The twist is about who shows up when there's a safety net. Imagine a swimming pool with no lifeguard: only strong swimmers jump in. Now post a lifeguard on duty and suddenly every overconfident uncle after three beers is doing cannonballs into the deep end. The lifeguard saves some of them, sure, but the total number of drowning incidents skyrockets. Safety nets don't just catch falling people — they invite people to walk the tightrope.

**Goal**
We need the answer that explains how rescue squads create MORE danger than they prevent. Something about their presence must change who decides to climb — and change it dramatically enough to overwhelm the lives they save.

**Answer choices**
**A. It is difficult to recruit and train members for the rescue squads.** — No Impact (4% of students)
"It's hard to find rescue volunteers!" Okay, but that is a totally different problem. The question is "why do rescue squads make things WORSE?" and this answer says "it's tough to hire people for rescue squads." That is like asking "why does eating at this restaurant make people sick?" and getting "they have trouble finding waitstaff." Maybe true, but spectacularly beside the point.

**B. The recording of deaths and injuries tends to be more accurate in mountain regions served by rescue squads.** — No Impact (8% of students)
"Maybe the numbers are just better-tracked where squads exist!" This is the LSAT equivalent of saying the scale is broken when the number is bad. The question asks us to take the paradox seriously — rescue squads are associated with MORE deaths — and explain why. Saying "well, maybe the data is skewed" is not a resolution; it is a refusal to engage. We need a real behavioral mechanism, not a statistical disclaimer.

**C. People who commonly take risks with their lives and health do not expect other people to take those risks to rescue them.** — Opposite (10% of students)
"Thrill-seekers climb no matter what!" Cool, but that is actually an argument FOR keeping rescue squads. If the adrenaline junkies are going to be reckless regardless, the only thing rescue squads change is whether someone comes to fish them out of a crevasse. Remove the squads and you get the SAME reckless climbers plus ZERO rescues. That is a recipe for MORE deaths, not fewer. This answer accidentally argues against the experienced climbers' position.

**D. Most of the people injured or killed while mountain climbing were not adequately prepared for the dangers they would face.** — No Distinction (13% of students)
"Most of the injured people were not prepared!" Yeah, we figured. That is like a detective announcing "the victim was killed by someone who wanted to kill them." We KNOW unprepared people are getting hurt. The question is WHY they are on the mountain in the first place. This answer gives us the crime scene report but forgets to identify the suspect. The missing piece — that rescue squads LURED these unprepared people into attempting the climb — is exactly what is NOT stated here.

**E. The lower the risk of climbing a particular mountain is perceived to be, the greater the number of less competent climbers who attempt to climb it.** — Correct (64% of students)
THIS is the money answer. Rescue squads are basically a neon sign saying "DON'T WORRY, WE'LL CATCH YOU!" And guess who reads that sign? Not the experienced climbers who know what they are doing. It is every overconfident amateur who watched a climbing documentary and thought "I could do that."

Without rescue squads, those people look at the mountain and think "that seems dangerous, maybe not." WITH rescue squads, they think "eh, worst case someone comes to get me." So the mountain goes from hosting 100 skilled climbers with 2 accidents to hosting 100 skilled climbers PLUS 500 clueless ones with 150 accidents, 50 rescues, and 100 casualties. The squads are saving people, but they are also the reason those people needed saving in the first place.

## S4 · Q20 — Agree/Disagree

**Correct answer:** A

### Stimulus
Paula: Earthlike planets seem to be the rule rather than the exception, so there probably are intelligent beings on other planets. Furthermore, we can expect our radio telescopes to detect signs of such beings. Alien scientists would have basically the same understanding of mathematics and physics that humans have. Thus they would inevitably discover gravity, electromagnetism, and other fundamental physical phenomena and then develop technologies such as radio communication.

Ashley: That is like saying they would inevitably have the same legal or political systems that humans do. Our science, mathematics, and technology are unique outgrowths of our physiology, cognitive makeup, and environment. Using radio telescopes to search for intelligent life is a waste of time and money.

### Prompt
The dialogue provides the most evidence that Paula and Ashley disagree with each other about whether

### Standard
**Paula**
There are lots of Earthlike planets out there, so there's probably intelligent life out there, and we should be able to find such life with radio telescopes. Other intelligent life would have basically the same math / physics that humans have. They'd discover the same fundamental forces of the universe and then develop radio communication.

**Ashley**
Saying they'd automatically have the same math / physics / radio technology is like saying (absurdly) that they'd have the same legal or political systems we do. All this stuff is a unique extension of the human form and the Earthly environment. Thus, using radio telescopes to find intelligent life would be pointless.

**Evaluate**
I often go claim-by-claim through the first person's statements to see if the 2nd person disagreed with any of the explicit claims.

Here, it seems like Ashley took issue with a couple claims:
- we can expect our radio telescopes to detect signs of such beings
(A would say, "that would be a waste of time and money")

- those smart aliens would have the same math, physics, and radio communication we have.
(A would say, "not necessarily — those are all just outgrowths of our unique physiology")

If we went down to the layer of assumptions, it feels like Paula assumes that "math / physics" are objective properties of the universe that all intelligent life would come to similar conclusions about. Ashley makes those discoveries sound more subjective or contingent on us being us.

**Goal**
Look for an answer about whether or not radio telescopes would be likely to detect intelligent life, about whether smart aliens would inevitably find the same (objective) math and physics and technology that we have or whether those things are unique properties of humanity.

**Answer choices**
**A. it is probable that there are intelligent alien beings who have developed radio communication** — Correct (60% of students)
This is the precise point where Paula and Ashley's positions directly conflict. Paula explicitly argues that intelligent aliens would probably develop radio communication — this is the foundation of her case for using radio telescopes. Ashley counters that our scientific and technological development, including radio, is a product of our unique cognitive makeup, implying that aliens would NOT necessarily develop radio. Paula would affirm this proposition; Ashley would deny it. Every other aspect of their arguments — the value of the search, the nature of intelligence, the role of biology — flows from this central factual dispute about whether alien species would arrive at radio technology.

**B. it is probable that there are intelligent alien beings who have the same legal or political systems that humans do** — No Support from Paula (8% of students)
Ashley mentions legal and political systems as an analogy to illustrate her broader point: just as it would be presumptuous to assume aliens have our legal systems, it is presumptuous to assume they have our science. This is a rhetorical device, not a substantive claim. Paula never addresses alien legal systems at all. For a genuine point of disagreement, both speakers must hold inferable positions on the topic that conflict with each other. Since Paula says nothing about alien legal systems and Ashley raises them only as an analogy, there is no actual dispute on this topic.

**C. our technology is influenced by our cognitive makeup** — Both Might Agree (11% of students)
Ashley's core thesis is that technology is shaped by a species' cognitive and physiological makeup — this is her explicit position. But Paula does not necessarily dispute this general principle. Paula could agree that cognition influences technology while still concluding that, despite cognitive differences, radio communication is a likely convergent development for any intelligent species. Their disagreement is about the specific outcome (whether aliens would develop radio), not about the general principle (whether cognition shapes technology). This answer identifies common ground rather than a point of conflict.

**D. there is likely to be intelligent life on other planets** — Out of Scope for Ashley (7% of students)
Paula assumes intelligent life exists on other planets and argues for a particular search method. Ashley's critique is conditional: even if intelligent aliens exist, we cannot assume they developed radio. She targets the search methodology, not the premise of alien existence. Ashley never expresses skepticism about whether intelligent life exists elsewhere — she simply thinks we are looking for it the wrong way. Without Ashley clearly denying alien existence, this is not a point of disagreement between the two speakers.

**E. scientists should spend more time and money on the search for intelligent extraterrestrial life** — Out of Scope for Both (14% of students)
Neither speaker takes a clear position on whether overall spending on searching for alien life should increase. While Ashley calls radio telescopes a "waste of time and money," this is a critique of the specific method, not a position on total research funding. She might support redirecting that money to different search technologies. Paula advocates for radio telescopes but never addresses total spending levels. For a point of disagreement, both speakers must hold inferable and conflicting positions. Their debate is about whether radio is the right approach, not about how much to budget for the search in general.

### Brief
**Paula's Position**
Earthlike planets probably host intelligent beings. These aliens would share our understanding of math and physics, so they would likely develop radio communication. Radio telescopes can detect their signals.

**Ashley's Position**
That is like saying aliens have the same legal and political systems. Science, math, and technology are unique outgrowths of our physiology. Searching with radio telescopes is a waste of time and money.

**Goal**
Identify the specific claim that Paula would affirm and Ashley would deny.

**Answer choices**
**A. it is probable that there are intelligent alien beings who have developed radio communication** — Correct (60% of students)
Paula says aliens would likely develop radio. Ashley says our technology reflects our unique cognition, implying aliens would NOT develop radio. This is exactly where their views collide.

**B. it is probable that there are intelligent alien beings who have the same legal or political systems that humans do** — No Support from Paula (8% of students)
Ashley mentions legal systems as an analogy, not as a genuine claim. Paula never addresses alien legal systems at all. Neither speaker actually debates this topic.

**C. our technology is influenced by our cognitive makeup** — Both Might Agree (11% of students)
Both speakers would likely accept that cognition shapes technology. Ashley says this explicitly, and Paula does not dispute it. They disagree about the outcome (radio), not this underlying premise.

**D. there is likely to be intelligent life on other planets** — Out of Scope for Ashley (7% of students)
Ashley does not dispute whether intelligent life exists elsewhere. Her argument assumes aliens might exist but challenges how we search for them, not whether they are out there.

**E. scientists should spend more time and money on the search for intelligent extraterrestrial life** — Out of Scope for Both (14% of students)
Neither speaker takes a clear position on whether overall spending on the search should increase. Their dispute is about method (radio telescopes), not budget.

### Another Way
**Paula's Position**
Paula stands up at the conference and says: "Aliens would totally invent radio! Math is math, physics is physics — any smart civilization figures out radio waves eventually. Let's point our radio telescopes at the sky!"

**Ashley's Position**
Ashley grabs the mic: "That is ridiculous. Radio is a HUMAN invention. Our whole science is shaped by our weird human brains. Aliens might communicate with smells, gravity pulses, or interpretive dance for all we know. Spending money listening for alien FM radio is a waste."

**Goal**
They agree aliens might exist. They agree aliens would be intelligent. But Paula thinks intelligence naturally leads to radio, while Ashley thinks intelligence could lead anywhere depending on biology. We need the specific proposition where one says yes and the other says no.

**Answer choices**
**A. it is probable that there are intelligent alien beings who have developed radio communication** — Correct (60% of students)
This is the heart of the fight. Paula: "Obviously aliens have radio. It is Science 101 for any intelligent species." Ashley: "Radio is as uniquely human as pizza and reality TV. Aliens might have something totally different."

It is like two people arguing about whether to set a trap using cheese. Paula says "every creature loves cheese!" Ashley says "cheese is a mammal thing — you are projecting your biology onto aliens who might eat rocks." The specific disagreement is whether the bait (radio) would actually attract the target (aliens). Everything else is downstream of this one question.

**B. it is probable that there are intelligent alien beings who have the same legal or political systems that humans do** — No Support from Paula (8% of students)
Ashley mentions legal systems the way someone mentions pizza when explaining something unrelated: "You know how every city has its own pizza style? Same idea with alien science." And this answer goes, "Aha! So they are arguing about PIZZA!" No. Ashley was making an analogy. Paula did not even acknowledge it. Nobody is actually debating whether aliens have a Supreme Court.

**C. our technology is influenced by our cognitive makeup** — Both Might Agree (11% of students)
This is like two chefs who both agree "ingredients determine the dish" but fight about whether every cuisine would independently invent pasta. The "ingredients matter" part is not the argument — it is the shared starting point. Paula and Ashley both accept that how a species thinks shapes what it builds. They just disagree about whether different thinkers would all end up building radios. Picking this as the disagreement is like identifying the one thing at a debate that both sides nod along to.

**D. there is likely to be intelligent life on other planets** — Out of Scope for Ashley (7% of students)
Neither Paula nor Ashley is wearing the "aliens are not real" hat. Ashley is not saying "there is nobody out there" — she is saying "there might be someone out there, but they are probably not listening to the radio." It is like two people planning a surprise party: they both agree the guest of honor exists, they just disagree about whether to call their cell phone or send a carrier pigeon. The existence of the guest is not the debate.

**E. scientists should spend more time and money on the search for intelligent extraterrestrial life** — Out of Scope for Both (14% of students)
This answer turns a scientific debate into a budget meeting nobody scheduled. Paula says "use radio telescopes." Ashley says "radio telescopes are a waste." Neither says "we should spend more" or "we should spend less" on alien-hunting in general. Ashley might happily redirect the radio telescope budget to alien smell-detection technology. They are fighting about the menu, not the check.

## S4 · Q21 — Strengthen

**Correct answer:** E

### Stimulus
Developer: The builders of the Glen Veil apartment complex will not complete the complex unless a road connecting it to the town of Sierra is built. The completed apartment complex would strengthen Sierra's economy, and a stronger economy would benefit every Sierra resident. Therefore, the residents of Sierra should vote in favor of a local tax to fund construction of the proposed road.

### Prompt
Which one of the following principles, if valid, would most help to justify the developer's reasoning?

### Standard
**Conclusion**
The residents of Sierra should vote in favor of a local tax to fund construction of the proposed road.

**Evidence**
If the proposed road connecting GVAC to Sierra isn't built, then the builders of GVAC won't complete the complex.

Were the complex to be completed, it would strengthen Sierra's economy and that would benefit every Sierra resident.

**Evaluate**
Why does the author think that residents of Sierra should vote in favor of a tax that would fund this proposed road? Ultimately, the author says, because it would benefit every Sierra resident (by making the economy stronger).

Naturally, increasing local taxes would also affect every Sierra resident, so there's an element of weighing tradeoffs going into this recommendation: you should vote to have a new tax imposed because the benefit you'll ultimately get from the stronger economy is worth it?

**Goal**
It's hard to predict what ideas they'll pair up in the correct answer choice.

When it comes to Premise facts, we know the proposed road
- is required to complete construction of something that, if constructed, would strengthen the economy / benefit everyone

When it comes to what the Conclusion wants to hear, it's ideas like
- this is a good tax to vote for
- we do want this apartment complex to be completed
- the benefit of the stronger economy would outweigh the harm of the new tax.

**Answer choices**
**A. If a construction project is necessary in order to strengthen a town's economy, then the residents of that town should vote in favor of a local tax to fund that construction project.** — Bad Trigger Match (21% of students)
This principle requires the project to be "necessary" for economic growth. The developer only claims the apartment complex would strengthen the economy, not that it is the only way to do so. The mismatch is between sufficiency and necessity. The developer argues the project is sufficient to produce benefits, but this principle demands that it be necessary — indispensable. Since other projects could also strengthen the economy, the developer cannot meet this principle's trigger condition. A principle requiring only that a project would benefit residents, rather than that it is indispensable, would be a better fit.

**B. The residents of a town should not vote in favor of a local tax to fund a construction project unless that construction project will produce results that benefit all of those residents.** — Opposite Logic (12% of students)
This principle states that residents should not vote for a tax increase unless the resulting benefits accrue to all residents. While the developer does claim the economy strengthening would benefit every resident, this principle is structured as a negative condition — a reason to vote no if the condition is not met, rather than a positive reason to vote yes when it is. More importantly, this principle could easily be weaponized against the developer: any resident who argues they would not personally benefit could use this principle to justify opposition. The developer needs a principle that positively connects benefit to voting obligation, not one that sets a high bar that could defeat the proposal.

**C. Whenever a town funds a construction project, it should do so by means of a tax rather than debt.** — Wrong Gap (11% of students)
This principle addresses whether projects should be funded by taxes versus debt — the method of financing. The developer's logical gap is not about which funding mechanism is best but about why residents should support this particular expenditure at all. A principle about taxation being preferable to borrowing does not bridge the gap between "you would benefit" and "you should vote for the tax." Even if taxes are the ideal funding method, this says nothing about why residents should approve this specific tax for this specific project. The principle operates in the wrong analytical domain entirely.

**D. Only those residents who will benefit from the results of a construction project should be required to pay a tax to fund that project.** — Undermines the Argument (1% of students)
This principle states that only those who benefit from a project should be required to pay for it. At first glance, this seems supportive — the developer claims residents benefit, so they should pay. But the principle creates a dangerous counter-argument. The developer wants all residents to vote yes. This principle implies that residents who do NOT benefit should NOT pay the tax. Any resident could argue "I will not personally benefit from apartments I will not live in," and this principle would support their opposition. Rather than unifying residents behind the tax, it fragments them into beneficiaries who should pay and non-beneficiaries who should not — undermining the developer's blanket appeal.

**E. Anyone who would benefit from the results of a construction project should vote in favor of a local tax to fund that project.** — Correct (54% of students)
This principle precisely fills the gap in the developer's argument. The developer establishes that residents would benefit from the project. This principle states that anyone who would benefit from a project should vote for the tax that funds it. Applied together: (1) the road enables an apartment complex that strengthens the economy (premise), (2) a stronger economy benefits every resident (premise), (3) anyone who benefits should vote for the funding tax (this principle), (4) therefore, residents should vote for the tax increase (conclusion). Without this principle, there is no logical reason why benefiting from something obligates you to support its funding. This principle provides that normative bridge, making the conclusion follow necessarily from the premises.

### Brief
**Conclusion**
Sierra's residents should vote for a tax increase to fund a new road.

**Evidence**
Builders will not complete an apartment complex unless the road is built. The completed complex would strengthen Sierra's economy and thereby benefit every resident.

**Goal**
Find the principle that, if accepted, would make the developer's conclusion follow logically from the premises. The gap is between "residents would benefit" and "residents should vote for the tax."

**Answer choices**
**A. If a construction project is necessary in order to strengthen a town's economy, then the residents of that town should vote in favor of a local tax to fund that construction project.** — Bad Trigger Match (21% of students)
This principle requires the project to be "necessary" for economic growth. The developer only claims the project would strengthen the economy, not that it is the only way to do so.

**B. The residents of a town should not vote in favor of a local tax to fund a construction project unless that construction project will produce results that benefit all of those residents.** — Opposite Logic (12% of students)
This principle says do not vote for a tax unless it benefits all residents. This could undermine the developer's argument if any residents fail to benefit, rather than justifying the conclusion.

**C. Whenever a town funds a construction project, it should do so by means of a tax rather than debt.** — Wrong Gap (11% of students)
Whether projects should be funded by taxes or debt is irrelevant. The developer's argument needs a reason why residents should vote for this tax, not a comparison of financing methods.

**D. Only those residents who will benefit from the results of a construction project should be required to pay a tax to fund that project.** — Undermines the Argument (1% of students)
If only beneficiaries should pay, any resident claiming not to benefit could use this principle to justify opposing the tax. It creates an exemption loophole rather than supporting the conclusion.

**E. Anyone who would benefit from the results of a construction project should vote in favor of a local tax to fund that project.** — Correct (54% of students)
The developer says residents would benefit. This principle says beneficiaries should vote for the funding tax. Combined: residents should vote for the tax. Perfect logical bridge from premises to conclusion.

### Another Way
**Conclusion**
Vote to raise your own taxes so I can build apartments. That is essentially the developer's pitch.

**Evidence**
The logical chain: your taxes pay for a road, I build apartments on that road, apartments boost the economy, economy boosting benefits you. Therefore... hand over your money?

**Evaluate**
It is actually a persuasive pitch, but there is a gap big enough to drive an apartment complex through. Just because something benefits you does not automatically mean you should vote to pay for it. Sunshine benefits everyone — should we vote to fund the sun? We need a principle that bridges "you will benefit" to "you should vote yes."

**Goal**
Find the general rule that, once accepted, transforms the developer's "this helps you" into an airtight "so you should pay for it." That missing bridge is the whole question.

**Answer choices**
**A. If a construction project is necessary in order to strengthen a town's economy, then the residents of that town should vote in favor of a local tax to fund that construction project.** — Bad Trigger Match (21% of students)
This principle basically says: "Vote yes ONLY if you absolutely, positively CANNOT improve the economy any other way." But the developer never said these apartments are humanity's last hope for economic growth. The argument is "this would help," not "without this we are doomed." Wrong threshold, wrong principle.

**B. The residents of a town should not vote in favor of a local tax to fund a construction project unless that construction project will produce results that benefit all of those residents.** — Opposite Logic (12% of students)
"Do not vote yes unless EVERYONE benefits." This principle is less like a bridge for the developer's argument and more like a trap door. Any curmudgeon can stand up at the town hall meeting and say "well, I do not see how I personally benefit," and suddenly this principle torpedoes the whole proposal. The developer needs "if you benefit, vote yes." This one says "if anyone does not benefit, vote no." That is the rhetorical equivalent of handing your opponent a loaded argument.

**C. Whenever a town funds a construction project, it should do so by means of a tax rather than debt.** — Wrong Gap (11% of students)
The developer's pitch: "This helps you, so vote for it!" The gap: why does "it helps me" mean "I should vote to pay for it"? This answer: "Well, taxes are better than debt." That is an entirely different discussion. It is like asking "should I marry this person?" and getting back "marriage is statistically better than common-law partnership for tax purposes." Technically about the same institution, completely irrelevant to the actual decision.

**D. Only those residents who will benefit from the results of a construction project should be required to pay a tax to fund that project.** — Undermines the Argument (1% of students)
Sounds reasonable at first: "You benefit? You pay!" But watch what happens when someone stands up at the town meeting and says, "Actually, I do not need more apartments, I do not shop at new stores, and I like the economy exactly as it is." This principle lets them off the hook. The developer wants a stampede toward the voting booth. This principle gives half the crowd a permission slip to stay home.

**E. Anyone who would benefit from the results of a construction project should vote in favor of a local tax to fund that project.** — Correct (54% of students)
The developer's argument has been building a highway of logic: road enables apartments, apartments boost economy, economy helps you. But then there is a canyon between "it helps you" and "so vote for it." Why should helping me mean I owe you my vote?

This principle builds the bridge: "If you benefit, you should vote yes." Drop that into the argument and the whole thing clicks together like the last puzzle piece. Simple, clean, and it transforms a persuasive pitch into an airtight argument.

## S4 · Q22 — Weaken

**Correct answer:** E

### Stimulus
Historian: Because medieval epistemology (theory of knowledge) is a complex subject, intellectual historians have, until recently, failed to produce a definition that would help to determine what should and what should not be included in it. Clearly, the solution is to define medieval epistemology simply as "the epistemological beliefs of the medieval epistemologists." That way, if we want to know whether medieval epistemology includes some epistemological claim, we just ask whether any medieval epistemologists believed it. If any did, it is part of medieval epistemology; if any medieval epistemologists believed the opposite, then that opposite claim is part of medieval epistemology.

### Prompt
Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the historian's argument?

### Standard
**Conclusion**
The solution for defining which things were believed by medieval epistemologists is to say it's "the epistemological beliefs of the medieval epistemologists".

**Evidence**
If any medieval epistemologists believed claim X, then we'll say "medieval epistemology believed X".

If any medieval epistemologists believed claim X was false, then we'll say "medieval epistemology did not believe X".

**Evaluate**
Won't this method lead to a bunch of contradictions, assuming that different medieval epistemologists probably believed different things.

If the 10 of them believed X was true and 10 of them believed the opposite were true, then following this author's plan we would say that "medieval epistemology both believed and didn't believe X".

**Goal**
Look for something pointing out this potential for self-contradictory statements about what medieval epistemology believed.

Or challenge the author's assumption that medieval epistemologists would have had unanimous consensus on beliefs, since that is the only way his plan would actually work.

**Answer choices**
**A. Medieval epistemologists held some of the same epistemological beliefs as did ancient epistemologists.** — Out of Scope (5% of students)
Whether medieval epistemologists shared beliefs with ancient epistemologists concerns the originality of their ideas, not the applicability of the proposed definition. Even if every belief they held was borrowed from antiquity, the definition still functions — you would identify the medieval epistemologists, catalog their beliefs, and end up with a medieval epistemology that mirrors the ancient version. Overlapping content between eras does not make the definition impossible to apply. This answer addresses the content of medieval epistemology, not the workability of the definition itself.

**B. The epistemological beliefs of medieval epistemologists depended upon their beliefs about nonepistemological matters.** — No Impact (15% of students)
This answer reveals that medieval epistemologists' beliefs were shaped by non-epistemological factors such as politics and religion. While historically illuminating, this does not challenge the proposed definition. The definition instructs us to identify medieval epistemologists and catalog their epistemological beliefs. The causes of those beliefs are irrelevant to this process. Even if every position they held was motivated by religious dogma rather than pure philosophical inquiry, those positions are still their epistemological beliefs. Knowing why they believed what they believed does not prevent us from identifying what they believed.

**C. The writings of most medieval epistemologists include passages that are clearly not about epistemology.** — No Impact (8% of students)
This answer points out that medieval epistemologists wrote about topics beyond epistemology, meaning their works contain mixed content. The implication is that applying the definition would require separating epistemological from non-epistemological material. But this is a manageable editorial task, not a fatal flaw. Scholars regularly distinguish between a thinker's epistemological claims and their ethical, metaphysical, or theological writings. The definition does not require that medieval epistemologists wrote only about epistemology — just that their epistemological beliefs can be identified within their broader work. The truly devastating weakness would be one showing the definition is logically impossible to apply, not merely that it requires careful reading.

**D. Some medieval epistemologists had epistemological beliefs that contradicted the epistemological beliefs of other medieval epistemologists.** — No Impact (38% of students)
If medieval epistemologists held contradictory beliefs, the proposed definition would simply produce a body of thought containing internal disagreements. But this is entirely normal for any intellectual tradition. Modern epistemology, ethics, physics — every discipline contains competing viewpoints among its practitioners. The definition explicitly accounts for this: if one epistemologist believed X and another believed the opposite, both are included. Internal contradiction is a feature of the definition, not a bug. This answer describes a consequence the historian already anticipated and accepted, not a problem that undermines the definition's applicability.

**E. There is much debate as to which medieval thinkers, if any, were epistemologists.** — Correct (34% of students)
This answer exposes the definition's fatal circularity. The definition says: medieval epistemology consists of the beliefs held by medieval epistemologists. To apply it, you must first identify who the medieval epistemologists were. But this answer reveals that there is significant scholarly debate about which medieval thinkers qualify as epistemologists. Resolving that debate requires a clear understanding of what medieval epistemology encompasses — the very thing the definition is supposed to provide. The result is a vicious circle: you need the definition's output (what medieval epistemology is) to generate its input (who the medieval epistemologists were). Without independent criteria for identifying medieval epistemologists, the definition cannot get off the ground.

### Brief
**Conclusion**
Medieval epistemology should be defined as the epistemological beliefs held by medieval epistemologists.

**Evidence**
Medieval epistemology is complex, and scholars have failed to produce a satisfactory definition. This proposed definition would include any belief held by any medieval epistemologist, even contradictory ones.

**Evaluate**
The definition is potentially circular: to apply it, you must first identify who the medieval epistemologists were, which may require already knowing what medieval epistemology is.

**Goal**
Find the answer that most effectively exposes or exploits this definitional weakness.

**Answer choices**
**A. Medieval epistemologists held some of the same epistemological beliefs as did ancient epistemologists.** — Out of Scope (5% of students)
Whether medieval and ancient epistemologists held the same beliefs is irrelevant. The definition's problem is about identifying who counts as a medieval epistemologist, not about the originality of their ideas.

**B. The epistemological beliefs of medieval epistemologists depended upon their beliefs about nonepistemological matters.** — No Impact (15% of students)
Medieval epistemologists being influenced by non-epistemological factors does not undermine the definition. You can still identify their epistemological beliefs regardless of what caused those beliefs.

**C. The writings of most medieval epistemologists include passages that are clearly not about epistemology.** — No Impact (8% of students)
Their writings mixing epistemological and non-epistemological content just means sorting through material. That is a practical inconvenience, not a fundamental definitional failure.

**D. Some medieval epistemologists had epistemological beliefs that contradicted the epistemological beliefs of other medieval epistemologists.** — No Impact (38% of students)
Epistemologists contradicting each other just means the field contained diverse views. The definition explicitly accommodates contradictions — that is normal for any intellectual tradition.

**E. There is much debate as to which medieval thinkers, if any, were epistemologists.** — Correct (34% of students)
If scholars cannot agree on who counts as a medieval epistemologist, the definition collapses. You need to identify the practitioners to apply it, but identifying practitioners requires already knowing what the field is — fatal circularity.

### Another Way
**Conclusion**
Someone thought they were being clever: "Medieval epistemology is whatever medieval epistemologists believed about epistemology." Sounds neat and tidy, right?

**Evidence**
The definition is motivated by frustration. Nobody can agree on what medieval epistemology IS, so this historian says: just look at what the practitioners believed. If they believed it, it counts. Contradictions welcome.

**Evaluate**
But here is the problem: to use this definition, you first need to identify the medieval epistemologists. And how do you know who they are unless you already know what medieval epistemology IS? It is the philosophical equivalent of needing work experience to get your first job, but needing a job to get work experience. The definition eats its own tail.

**Goal**
We need the answer that best exposes this circular trap — the one that shows why you cannot get the definition off the ground in the first place.

**Answer choices**
**A. Medieval epistemologists held some of the same epistemological beliefs as did ancient epistemologists.** — Out of Scope (5% of students)
"Medieval thinkers just recycled ancient Greek ideas!" Okay, but that does not break the definition. If someone defines "my Spotify playlist" as "songs I added to my playlist," the definition still works perfectly even if every song is a cover of a Beatles track. The content being unoriginal does not make the definition impossible to use. We need an answer that makes the definition collapse under its own weight, not one that makes the results unimpressive.

**B. The epistemological beliefs of medieval epistemologists depended upon their beliefs about nonepistemological matters.** — No Impact (15% of students)
"Their epistemology was influenced by religion and politics!" Name a philosopher whose was not. But more importantly, this does not make the definition stop working. If someone defines "Nicole's cooking" as "dishes Nicole makes," finding out Nicole was influenced by her Italian grandmother does not somehow make the definition unworkable. The causal backstory behind the beliefs is completely separate from whether we can identify and catalog them.

**C. The writings of most medieval epistemologists include passages that are clearly not about epistemology.** — No Impact (8% of students)
"They wrote about other stuff too!" And? This is like saying a cookbook is hard to use because the author also included personal anecdotes between recipes. You just skip to the recipes. Yes, medieval philosophers wrote about theology, politics, and probably lunch. But you can still pull out their epistemological views. The definition's real problem is not that the source material is messy — it is something far more fundamental than a sorting exercise.

**D. Some medieval epistemologists had epistemological beliefs that contradicted the epistemological beliefs of other medieval epistemologists.** — No Impact (38% of students)
Breaking news: people who think for a living sometimes think different things. If we disqualified every field whose practitioners disagreed, we would have to shut down philosophy, economics, medicine, and basically every department at every university. The definition ALREADY says contradictions are welcome — "if any believed the opposite, that is included too." This answer is pointing out a feature the historian explicitly designed into the system. It is like critiquing an umbrella for getting wet.

**E. There is much debate as to which medieval thinkers, if any, were epistemologists.** — Correct (34% of students)
This is the answer that makes the whole definition implode. Watch the logic eat itself:

"What is medieval epistemology?" "It is what medieval epistemologists believed!" "Great, who were the medieval epistemologists?" "The people who practiced medieval epistemology!" "...which is defined as...?" "What medieval epistemologists believed!"

And THIS answer twists the knife: scholars cannot even agree on who qualifies as a medieval epistemologist. So the definition is like a recipe that says "add the right amount of the correct ingredient" — completely useless unless you already have the answer. It is a philosophical Catch-22, and this answer drags it into the spotlight.

## S4 · Q23 — Flaw

**Correct answer:** E

### Stimulus
Official: Six months ago, the fines for parking violations on the city's streets were raised to help pay for the parking garage that had just opened. Since then, parking violations on our streets have dropped by 50 percent. Hence, if we want there to be even fewer parking violations, the fines should be raised again.

### Prompt
The reasoning in the official's argument is flawed in that the argument

### Standard
**Conclusion (Hence)**
If we want there to be even fewer parking violations, the fines should be raised again.

**Evidence**
Six months ago we raised the fines for parking violations, and since then parking violations on our streets have dropped by 50%.

**Evaluate**
A common trope in Logical Reasoning is to say, "Policy change X went into effect. Then thing Y happened. So, apparently policy change X caused thing Y."

It seems here that our author is definitely making that same causal assumption, that the increase in fines is the cause of the 50% drop in parking violations.

The conclusion has implicit causality. When you say, "If you want X, you should do Y", you're implying that Y can bring about X.

This is the classic Explain Curious Fact argument structure, and when it shows up on Flaw, it means that they are usually just testing our awareness that the author has overconfidently arrived at one possible explanation for a curious fact, even though others could exist.

**Goal**
So we might see answers saying, "The author takes for granted that because X was followed by Y, X caused Y" or "the author fails to consider other things could have caused there to be 50% fewer parking violations (a pandemic or storm that led to there being fewer people out and about, or maybe an increase in visibility of meter maids making people worry about whether they still had value left on their meter).

But there's also a prediction aspect to the conclusion, so even if we thought the fines were the causal reason that violations dropped by 50%, we won't necessarily get a further reduction by increasing fines even more. At a certain point, you've already maxed out the disincentive to get a parking violation. Whether it's a $500 or $600 fine, I'm equally determined to not get that ticket.

**Answer choices**
**A. takes a possible effect of a reduction to be a possible cause of that reduction** — Wrong Flaw Type (21% of students)
Confusing cause and effect means reversing the causal direction — claiming X caused Y when actually Y caused X. The argument's timeline is straightforward and correct: fines were raised, then violations decreased. There is no reversal of the causal arrow. The actual flaw is different: the argument ignores a confounding variable (the parking garage) that could explain the same outcome. This is an alternative-cause error, not a reversed-causation error. The argument gets the temporal sequence right but fails to consider that another simultaneous change might be the real explanation. These are distinct logical errors, and this answer identifies the wrong one.

**B. takes for granted that raising fines a second time will reduce parking violations at least as much as it did the first time** — Secondary Concern (10% of students)
This answer identifies a real but secondary issue: diminishing returns. Perhaps the first fine increase captured the "easy wins" — the most price-sensitive violators — and a second increase would affect fewer people. But this critique is premature. The primary flaw is more fundamental: the argument has not established that fines caused the initial decrease at all. The parking garage is an unexamined alternative explanation. Before questioning whether a second dose of medicine will work as well as the first, we should first confirm the first dose was actually medicine and not a placebo. This answer skips ahead to a secondary objection while missing the foundational problem.

**C. fails to take into account the financial benefits the city is now deriving from fines for parking violations** — Irrelevant Objection (2% of students)
This answer introduces a cost-benefit analysis: do the revenues from fines justify the costs of enforcement? But the argument's conclusion is about effectiveness ("raise fines to reduce violations further"), not about profitability ("raise fines to make money"). The logical flaw lies in the causal reasoning — attributing the decrease in violations to fines while ignoring the garage. Whether fines are financially worthwhile is a completely separate question from whether they actually caused the behavioral change. This answer operates in the wrong analytical framework for a flaw question about causal reasoning.

**D. takes for granted that people who park their cars illegally would prefer to park legally** — Not Assumed (3% of students)
This answer claims the flaw is assuming illegal parkers would prefer to park legally. But the argument's logic relies on deterrence through financial punishment, not on changing people's parking preferences. Deterrence works even when people prefer the illegal option — they choose the legal option to avoid the fine, not because they like it better. The argument does not need to assume anything about preferences; it only needs to assume fines change behavior through the threat of cost. The actual flaw is much simpler and more fundamental: the argument ignores that the new parking garage, not the fines, might explain the reduced violations.

**E. fails to establish that the initial decrease in parking violations was not due to the availability of additional parking spaces** — Correct (64% of students)
This is the classic alternative-cause or confounding-variable flaw. Two events occurred simultaneously: the fine increase and the garage opening. Violations decreased by 50%. The argument attributes the decrease entirely to the fine increase and recommends a second increase. But it fails to consider that the parking garage — which provided new legal parking spaces — could be the actual explanation. People may have stopped parking illegally because they finally had a convenient legal option, not because they feared costlier tickets. Without controlling for this alternative cause, the argument's causal attribution is unjustified, and its recommendation (raise fines again) rests on an unproven foundation.

### Brief
**Conclusion**
Parking fines should be raised again to further reduce violations.

**Evidence**
When fines for parking violations were raised to help pay for a newly opened parking garage, violations dropped by 50%.

**Evaluate**
Two changes happened simultaneously: fines increased AND a new garage opened. The argument credits only the fines for the improvement, ignoring that the garage gave people a legal place to park.

**Goal**
Find the answer that identifies this alternative-cause flaw — the failure to consider that the parking garage, not the fine increase, may explain the drop in violations.

**Answer choices**
**A. takes a possible effect of a reduction to be a possible cause of that reduction** — Wrong Flaw Type (21% of students)
The argument does not reverse cause and effect. The timeline is correct: fines increased, then violations dropped. The flaw is ignoring an alternative cause (the garage), not confusing the causal direction.

**B. takes for granted that raising fines a second time will reduce parking violations at least as much as it did the first time** — Secondary Concern (10% of students)
Whether a second fine increase would be equally effective is a secondary concern. The primary flaw is more basic: the argument has not proven the first increase caused the improvement at all.

**C. fails to take into account the financial benefits the city is now deriving from fines for parking violations** — Irrelevant Objection (2% of students)
Whether fines generate enough revenue to justify enforcement costs is an economic question, not a logical flaw in the causal reasoning about what reduced violations.

**D. takes for granted that people who park their cars illegally would prefer to park legally** — Not Assumed (3% of students)
The argument does not assume illegal parkers prefer legal parking. It argues that higher fines deter through punishment, not through changing preferences. This misidentifies the argument's reasoning.

**E. fails to establish that the initial decrease in parking violations was not due to the availability of additional parking spaces** — Correct (64% of students)
The garage opened when fines increased. The drop in violations could be due to the garage providing legal parking, not the fines. The argument ignores this alternative explanation and wrongly credits fines alone.

### Another Way
**Conclusion**
The fines are working! Let us raise them MORE!

**Evidence**
The city raises parking fines AND opens a shiny new parking garage on the same day. Violations drop by half.

**Evaluate**
That is like starting a diet and a gym membership on the same Monday, losing 20 pounds, and telling everyone "my diet is incredible — I should eat even LESS!" Meanwhile, the gym membership is standing in the corner going "HELLO?! I HELPED TOO!" The argument completely ignores the giant concrete alternative explanation sitting right there with 500 empty parking spaces. Maybe people stopped parking illegally because they finally had somewhere legal to park, not because they were terrified of bigger fines.

**Goal**
We need the answer that calls out this blind spot — the failure to consider the garage as the real explanation.

**Answer choices**
**A. takes a possible effect of a reduction to be a possible cause of that reduction** — Wrong Flaw Type (21% of students)
"Confusing cause and effect" would be like saying "fewer violations caused the fines to go up." That is backwards, and nobody is arguing that. The timeline is clear: fines up, violations down. The problem is not WHICH came first — it is that there is a giant parking garage that ALSO happened at the same time and could be the real reason. This is like accusing a detective of getting the time of death wrong when actually they arrested the wrong person.

**B. takes for granted that raising fines a second time will reduce parking violations at least as much as it did the first time** — Secondary Concern (10% of students)
This answer says "maybe the second fine increase will not work as well as the first!" Fair point — but we have not even established that the FIRST one worked. It is like a film critic debating whether a sequel will match the original's box office when the original's success might have been entirely due to the holiday release window. Worry about the sequel later; first, figure out if the original actually did what it claimed to do.

**C. fails to take into account the financial benefits the city is now deriving from fines for parking violations** — Irrelevant Objection (2% of students)
This answer wants to do a cost-benefit analysis when we are looking for a logical flaw. It is like critiquing a rain dance by asking "is it worth the cost of the costumes?" when the real question is "DID THE DANCE CAUSE THE RAIN?" The argument's problem is not that fines are an inefficient revenue source. The problem is that fines might not have done anything at all — the garage might deserve all the credit. Wrong lens, wrong answer.

**D. takes for granted that people who park their cars illegally would prefer to park legally** — Not Assumed (3% of students)
Do illegal parkers dream of legal spots? Probably not — that is kind of why they park illegally. But that is not the argument's assumption. Deterrence does not require preference change; it just requires "this ticket costs enough that I will walk an extra block." The real flaw is not some deep psychological assumption about parking preferences — it is the massive, obvious, impossible-to-miss parking garage that opened at the exact same time.

**E. fails to establish that the initial decrease in parking violations was not due to the availability of additional parking spaces** — Correct (64% of students)
Imagine starting to wear a lucky hat AND studying harder on the same day. Your test scores improve. You conclude: "The hat is magic! I need an even LUCKIER hat!" Meanwhile, the studying is obviously responsible.

That is this argument in a nutshell. Fines go up and a garage opens simultaneously. Violations drop. The argument says "fines did it — raise them more!" completely ignoring the 500-space concrete rectangle that just gave everyone a legal place to park. The argument does not even mention the garage as a possible explanation, which is the logical equivalent of ignoring the elephant in the parking lot.
